summary.text: A rainbow is a multicolored circular arc in the sky, made when water droplets refract, internally reflect and disperse light.
Sunlight rainbows always appear opposite the sun, so you see one with the sun behind you and water drops in front of you.
In the main bow red sits on the outer edge and violet on the inner, and a second bow about 10° outside shows the colors reversed.

facts.label: Double rainbow
facts.value: Second arc appears about 10° outside the first

facts.label: Full circles
facts.value: Visible from an aeroplane when there is enough mist

facts.label: Polarization
facts.value: Light of the primary arc is 96% polarised

facts.label: Moonbows
facts.value: Often look white because night color vision is poor

items.prompt: It is early morning, the sun is low, and a shower is passing. Which way should you look for a rainbow?

options.label: Toward the sun in the east
Straight overhead
Toward the south
Away from the sun, toward the west

items.explain: Sunlight rainbows appear in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun, so morning rainbows are usually in the west.

items.prompt: A child paints a rainbow and asks which stripe goes along the outer edge of the arc. What is right for a main bow?

options.label: Violet
Red
Green
Yellow

items.explain: In a primary rainbow, red is on the outer part of the arc and violet on the inner side.

items.prompt: On a dry, sunny afternoon you stand with the sun behind you and spray a hose into the air ahead. What may happen?

options.label: Nothing, since rainbows need real rainclouds
Only a white glow, never any colors
A rainbow appears in the spray
A rainbow appears only if the water is cold

items.explain: Rainbows can be caused by mist, spray and other airborne water, and can be created by dispersing droplets on a sunny day.

items.prompt: On a bright moonlit night a faint arc shows up, but it looks white rather than colored. What is the best explanation?

options.label: Moonlight contains no colors at all
The droplets freeze at night, which removes the color
Our eyes see color poorly in low light
The arc is a different kind of cloud than a rainbow

items.explain: Moonbows can occur on strongly moonlit nights, and since human color perception is poor in low light they are often seen as white.

items.prompt: Looking at a rainbow, you notice the sky inside the arc is brighter than the sky outside it. Why?

options.label: Drops scatter light over a disc that mostly overlaps into white
Raindrops give off their own light inside the arc
Clouds are always thinner on the inner side of the bow
Violet light is stronger than red light overall

items.explain: Each spherical drop scatters light over a disc in the sky. Over most of it all wavelengths overlap to white light, and the colors appear only at the edge.

items.prompt: A child counts seven stripes in a rainbow and asks whether nature has exactly seven colors. What is the best answer?

options.label: Yes, seven is fixed by the physics of the water drops
No, the stripes are a product of our perception and the count is a choice
Yes, but only in rainbows seen from high mountains
No, a rainbow has exactly five distinct colors

items.explain: The apparent discreteness of main colors is an artefact of human perception. Newton settled on seven partly by analogy with musical notes.

paragraphs.heading: What a rainbow is
paragraphs.text: A rainbow appears when water droplets refract, internally reflect and disperse light, leaving a continuous spectrum in the sky. It takes the shape of a circular arc of many colors. Rain is not the only source: mist, spray and airborne dew can make one too.

paragraphs.heading: Where to look
paragraphs.text: A rainbow made by sunlight always sits in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun. You need drops of water in the air and sunshine coming from behind you at a low angle. That is why rainbows usually show up in the western sky in the morning and the eastern sky in the early evening. The center of the arc always lies on the line running from the Sun to your eye.

paragraphs.heading: Inside a droplet
paragraphs.text: In the main, or primary, rainbow, light bends as it enters a drop, reflects off the back of the drop, and bends again as it leaves. Red ends up on the outer edge of the arc and violet on the inner edge. Each round drop scatters light over a whole circular disc of sky, and red light is spread over a wider angle than blue. Over most of that disc all the colors overlap into white light, so the sky inside the bow looks brighter than outside; at the disc's edge do the colors separate into a rainbow.

paragraphs.heading: Double rainbows
paragraphs.text: In good conditions, a second, larger but fainter arc often shows up about 10° outside the first. Its colors run the other way, with red on its lower side. The best displays come when half the sky is still dark with rain clouds while the sky toward the Sun is clear where you stand. The bright bow then stands out against the dark background.

paragraphs.heading: Full circles and moonbows
paragraphs.text: From the ground a rainbow usually looks like an arc, but from an aeroplane, with enough mist, you can sometimes see a full circle. This can be confused with a glory, though a glory is usually far smaller, covering only 5–20°. On strongly moonlit nights a moonbow can rarely appear. Because people see color poorly in low light, it often looks white.

paragraphs.heading: How many colors
paragraphs.text: The best-known list is Isaac Newton's seven: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, recalled as Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain. Newton first named only five main colors, in 1672, then added orange and indigo to match the number of notes in a musical scale. Today the bow is often split into red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue and violet instead. The way the bands seem distinct is an artefact of human perception. Settling on an exact number of main colors is a somewhat arbitrary choice.

paragraphs.heading: Catching one on camera
paragraphs.text: Fitting the whole half-circle of a rainbow into one photo is hard, because it needs an 84° angle of view. On a 35 mm camera that means a wide-angle lens whose focal length is 19 mm or shorter. Now that software can stitch overlapping photos into a panorama, pictures of the entire arc, and even the second arc, are fairly easy to make.
